reels.outcome: By the end of this post, viewers will be able to push back on absorbing a departed coworker's job by asking what should pause.

loops.open: Your coworker quit. Why is their job now yours?
loops.payoff: Because quits are common: 3.1 million Americans quit in August 2026 (BLS), and the work lands on whoever stays.
You don't have to silently take it all: ask which of your work pauses.

sources: https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/jolts_09292026.htm (BLS JOLTS: the number of quits was 3.1 million in August 2026)

carousels.outcome: By the end of this post, viewers will know a repeatedly canceled 1:1 is a pattern worth fixing and be able to ask for a short, specific meeting their boss can say yes to.

loops.open: Your 1:1 got canceled again. What is it really telling you?
loops.payoff: It's become a pattern: moved, then canceled again.
Yes: managers account for at least 70% of the variance in team engagement (Gallup).

loops.open: So what does skipping you say?
loops.payoff: Often overload, not dislike, but the pattern still costs you.
Not waiting quietly to be rescheduled.
Ask for 15 minutes on a set day with two specific questions.

sources: https://news.gallup.com/businessjournal/182792/managers-account-variance-employee-engagement.aspx (Gallup: managers account for at least 70% of the variance in employee engagement scores across business units)

slides.text: "Something came up." Moved to next week. *Then canceled again.* Does it matter?
Managers drive at least 70% of team engagement differences. *So what does skipping you say?*
Often it's overload, not dislike. *But the pattern costs you.* So what helps?
Waiting quietly to be rescheduled. *Out of sight, out of mind.* What works instead?
"Can we keep 15 minutes Thursday? I need your call on two things."
